originality.rationale: The exact score identity for arbitrary Gaussian covariance and optimum scalar noise-weighted fit are prior work (Xie 2026 Theorem 4.1 and Appendix C.3); the elliptical Gaussian quadratic moment transform is classical (DLMF 19.31). The surviving result specifically quantifies a strict component-order reversal with logarithmically diverging gain ratio despite vanishing relative scalar approximation error for a single polar-normalized noise family. Relevant mathematical primary passages were read; the simultaneous asymptotic comparison was not stated in them. Older general projected-normal literature poses a nontrivial bibliographic residual risk.
residual_risks: Older directional-statistics literature, including Wang and Gelfand (2013) and Pukkila and Rao (1988), may implicitly or explicitly derive equivalent specialized response limits; not all original full texts were accessible.

The general Gaussian score identity and scalar-fit criterion are already published. Only the quantitative joint asymptotic and strict inversion, rather than general construction, are evaluated as new.

value.rationale: The source explicitly motivates scalar noise-response matching, but warns that covariance-weighted averages can hide errors in low-noise directions. This theorem supplies an exact, all-parameter and logarithmically sharp witness in the original polar update model: positive local-signal coordinate rankings reverse, response conditioning diverges, and the best scalar diagnostic tends to zero. That coupled separation matters for interpreting calibration metrics and is not just a Taylor exercise or computation of an arbitrary integral.
